Michigan lawmakers are the closest they’ve been in years to passing a statewide septic code that would increase inspections to guard against human fecal waste leaking into the state’s lakes, rivers, and groundwater. The Democrat-controlled state Senate is poised to pass the measure after nearly four decades of advocacy and negotiations. But the bill’s future in the state House is unclear, with local officials raising familiar concerns about implementation and private property rights. Michigan is the only state in the nation without uniform requirements for onsite septic construction, maintenance, and inspection. Instead, each of the state’s 45 health departments employs its own rules. Many have no inspection requirements after the initial installation. SB 771 would change that, directing the state’s department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) to issue a set of septic regulations to periodically inspect the over 1.3 million onsite septic systems in the state. After a ramp-up period, each system would be inspected every 10 years. Circle of Blue WaterNews Weekly water news delivered directly to your inbox The Stream Global water news delivered twice a week. They were then referred to a House committee but received no further action. Onsite septic systems, which the bill would regulate, are backyard tanks and drain fields that filter fecal waste for around one third of Michiganders who are not connected to a city sewer system. Well-maintained systems can successfully filter out E. coli and other bacteria and contaminants that can pose harm to both human health and the environment. Improperly maintained systems can leach contaminants into groundwater. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency recommends most household septic systems be inspected “at least every three years” and says they are typically pumped every three to five years.
